reading.rtitle: The Sentence That Earns Its Detail
paras: In an interview, the strongest answers are not the longest ones. They are the ones that carry the most detail in the fewest sentences. Compare two candidates. The first says: 'I worked with an engineer. She built our data pipeline. She left the company last year.' The second says: 'The engineer who built our data pipeline left the company last year.' Same three facts, one sentence. The tool that makes this possible is the relative clause, and it is the quiet engine of professional English.

A relative clause begins with who, that, which, whose or where, and it attaches extra information to a noun. There are two kinds, and the difference is a pair of commas. A defining clause tells the listener which one you mean, and it takes no commas: 'The bottleneck that slowed every release was in the review step.' Remove the clause and the sentence loses its meaning. A non-defining clause adds information about someone the listener has already identified, and it sits between commas: 'My counterpart in Dublin, who runs the same platform, reports the same numbers.' Remove it and the sentence still works. One rule never bends: 'that' is never used in a non-defining clause.

Two more habits separate a fluent speaker from a careful one. First, when the relative pronoun is the object of the clause, you can simply drop it: 'The workaround we used for six months has finally been retired.' Fluent speakers do this constantly, and it makes speech sound lighter and faster. Second, never repeat the noun inside the clause. 'The system that we replaced it' says the same thing twice, because the relative pronoun has already done that job. Get those two habits right and your answers will sound the way a senior person sounds: dense with detail, and short.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: Relative clauses should be avoided in interviews because they make sentences too long.
Relative clauses pack several facts into one sentence, and a pair of commas separates the defining kind from the non-defining kind.
The words 'that' and 'which' can always be used in exactly the same places.

gapfill.text: who = people. that / which = things. whose = possession (his, her, their). where = places. Commas change everything: no commas means the clause says WHICH one you mean; commas mean the clause is extra information, and there you use who or which -- never that.

bank.label: Useful sentences for describing a team
items: The engineer who designed our first pipeline still mentors every new hire.
The bottleneck that slowed every release was in the review step.
The lab where the models are tested is in Zurich.
The two teams whose turnover was highest are now the most stable.
My counterpart in Dublin, who runs the same platform, reports the same numbers.
The review step, which was fully manual until March, is now automated.
The workaround we used for six months has finally been retired.
The group we consolidated in March owns the release pipeline now.

forms.title: Six ways to attach a detail to a noun
cards: 'The engineer who designed our first pipeline still mentors new hires.' No commas: the clause says WHICH engineer.
'The bottleneck that slowed every release was in the review step.' Both are correct here; 'that' sounds more spoken.
'The two teams whose turnover was highest are now the most stable.' It replaces his, her, their.
'The lab where the models are tested is in Zurich.' Simpler and far more natural than 'in which'.
'My counterpart in Dublin, who runs the same platform, reports the same numbers.' Commas on both sides, and never 'that'.
When the clause has its own subject
'The workaround we used lasted six months.' Drop the pronoun when it is the OBJECT of the clause -- never when it is the subject.

items.situation: A recruiter asks which project you are proudest of. Name it in one sentence with a defining clause.
tips: The project that removed the bottleneck in our review step is the one I am proudest of.
The system we consolidated last year cut three approvals down to one.

items.situation: Introduce a colleague the interviewer has never heard of, in one sentence.
tips: The engineer who designed our first pipeline still mentors every new hire.
The person who owns that platform reports directly to me.

items.situation: Add extra information about someone the interviewer already knows. Watch the commas.
tips: My counterpart in Dublin, who runs the same platform, reports the same numbers.
My director, who joined in 2019, approved the plan in one meeting.

items.situation: Describe the place where something happens, in one sentence.
tips: The lab where the models are tested is in Zurich.
The room where we run the reviews holds twelve people.

items.situation: Talk about a team by something that belongs to it. Use whose.
tips: The two teams whose turnover was highest are now the most stable.
The group whose workaround we retired is fully automated now.

items: Round 1 -- Guided
In three sentences, describe your current team: one defining clause with who, one with that, and one with where.
Round 2 -- The team profile
Give a one-minute profile of a real team: who owns what, which problem was fixed, and where the work happens.
Round 3 -- Add the extra detail
Deliver the same profile again, adding two non-defining clauses between commas -- and drop the pronoun once, where it is the object.
Curveball
The interviewer asks 'And who exactly reported to you?' Answer with one defining clause, then one non-defining clause about the same person.

answerkey.title: Reveal the model profile
list: Model: 'The team that owns our release pipeline is the group we consolidated in March. The engineer who designed the first version still mentors everyone we onboard. The bottleneck that slowed every release was in the review step, and the review step, which was fully manual until March, is now automated. The lab where the models are tested has doubled its capacity. The two teams whose turnover was highest last year are now the most stable in the division, and the workaround we used for six months has finally been retired. My counterpart in Dublin, who runs the same platform in Europe, is copying the model to scale it.'
Defining with who: The engineer who designed the first version...
Defining with that: The bottleneck that slowed every release... / The team that owns our release pipeline...
Defining with where: The lab where the models are tested...
Defining with whose: The two teams whose turnover was highest...
Non-defining, between commas: ...the review step, which was fully manual until March, is now automated. / My counterpart in Dublin, who runs the same platform in Europe, ...
Pronoun dropped (object): the group we consolidated in March / the workaround we used for six months
answerkey.note: No commas = the clause tells the listener WHICH one. Commas = the clause is extra information, and there you use who or which, never that. Drop the pronoun only when it is the object of the clause, and never repeat the noun inside it.

listenings.text: Let me introduce the group that owns this platform, because most of you have only seen their names on a slide. The engineer who designed the first version of the pipeline is Priya, and she now mentors every person we onboard. The bottleneck that used to slow every release was in the review step, and the team that fixed it did the work in eleven days. Our lab in Zurich, where the models are tested before release, has doubled its capacity this year. My counterpart in Dublin, who runs the same platform for the European market, reports exactly the numbers we do. And the two groups whose turnover was highest last year are now the most stable in the division, because we consolidated them into one team with a single manager. The workaround we used for six months has finally been retired. That is the group. Ask them anything.

Here is the test I give every candidate, and it takes two seconds. Say the sentence out loud, then take the clause away and listen to what is left. If the sentence still tells me exactly which person or which system you mean, the clause was extra information, so it needs commas around it, and you must use who or which, never that. My counterpart in Dublin, who joined last year, runs the same platform. Take that clause out and you still know who I mean. But if the sentence suddenly becomes vague, the clause was doing real work, so no commas at all. The engineer who built the pipeline has left. Take that clause out and nobody knows which engineer. One more thing. In an interview, most of your clauses will be the defining kind, because you are naming projects, teams and people that nobody in that room has ever heard of.
